title: Narrow-Sense Type-III Dirac Cones and Additional Flat Lines on a Honeycomb Lattice with Anisotropic Next-Nearest-Neighbor Hoppings
abstract: Critically tilted Dirac cones have attracted considerable attention because of their unconventional electronic properties in two-dimensional massless Dirac-fermion systems. Among them, the narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone is characterized by a flat dispersion along the direction connecting the two Dirac points.   Using a tight-binding model on a single-orbital honeycomb lattice, we demonstrate that narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones can be realized by tuning anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. Type-I and type-II Dirac cones emerge on either side of the critical point, enabling a systematic investigation of the electronic properties across the type-I, narrow-sense type-III, and type-II regimes.   We further find that the present model exhibits additional flat lines in momentum space whose energy coincides with the Dirac-point energy at the narrow-sense type-III critical point. This band structure produces a pronounced enhancement of the density of states at the Fermi energy and, consequently, a substantial enhancement of the electronic specific heat compared with that expected for an ideal narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone. Our results show that the honeycomb lattice with anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings provides a simple platform for exploring unconventional thermodynamic properties arising from the energy coincidence of narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones and additional flat lines at the Fermi energy.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes a honeycomb lattice model to show how anisotropic hopping can generate narrow-sense Type-III Dirac cones. Crucially, the model also predicts additional flat energy lines at the critical point, which leads to a pronounced enhancement of the electronic density of states and specific heat compared to ideal Dirac cone predictions.
main_problem: The study investigates the realization of narrow-sense Type-III Dirac cones and the emergence of additional flat lines in the band structure of a honeycomb lattice.
main_result: The model demonstrates that anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings can induce narrow-sense Type-III Dirac cones, and the co-existence of these cones with additional flat lines significantly enhances the density of states and electronic specific heat.
method: The analysis employs a tight-binding model approach, calculating the energy dispersion, density of states (DOS), and electronic specific heat ($C$) by tuning the hopping anisotropy ratio.
model_or_system: The system is a single-orbital honeycomb lattice described by a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating nearest-neighbor and anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hopping terms. The electronic properties are analyzed across Type-I, narrow-sense Type-III, and Type-II Dirac cone regimes.
key_observables: Dirac cone type (I, III, II), Density of States (DOS), Electronic Specific Heat ($C$), and the existence/energy of additional flat lines.
important_parameters: The ratio of anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hopping to nearest-neighbor hopping ($t'/t$), particularly around the critical point $t'/t = 0.5$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a single-orbital tight-binding model approximation for the electronic structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy bands for different cone types, the dependence of the DOS and specific heat on the anisotropy ratio, and the local character of energy extrema (saddle points) at high-symmetry points.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian, first establishing the realization of Type-III cones, then detailing the appearance of additional flat lines at the critical point, and finally quantifying the resulting enhancement in thermodynamic properties like the specific heat.
why_interesting: The finding that geometric features (flat lines) can dramatically enhance thermodynamic responses (specific heat) near a critical point is a general concept relevant to understanding quantum criticality in various condensed matter systems.
